topics.name: Inflation
topics.summary: How prices across an economy are measured, why they rise, and what central banks aim for.

cards.title: What Inflation Measures
cards.definition: Inflation is a broad, sustained rise in the prices of goods and services across an economy. Because each unit of currency then buys less than it did before, inflation is best understood as a loss of purchasing power rather than as any single price going up.
cards.example: A household filling the same grocery cart in June 2022 as a year earlier paid roughly 9 percent more for it. Nothing in the cart had changed; the money had.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Consumer Price Index
cards.definition: The Consumer Price Index measures the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of goods and services. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes it monthly, and the basket's weights come from a survey of what households actually buy.
cards.example: The basket is not a metaphor. Price collectors record the cost of specific items in specific stores every month, sorted into 8 major groups: food and beverages, housing, apparel, transportation, medical care, recreation, education and communication, and other goods and services.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.documentTitle: Consumer Price Index Frequently Asked Questions

cards.title: Core and Headline Inflation
cards.definition: Headline inflation covers every category, food and energy included. Core inflation excludes food and energy, whose prices swing sharply with weather, harvests, and global energy markets. Core is used as a guide to the underlying trend, not as a better measure of what households actually pay.
cards.example: A driver watching pump prices fall and a central banker watching core inflation can both be right in the same month. The FOMC states its 2 percent goal for the personal consumption expenditures price index, and reads the core version of it to judge where the trend is heading.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.observationPeriod: FOMC longer-run goal, in force since January 2012

cards.title: Demand-Pull Inflation
cards.definition: Demand-pull inflation happens when spending grows faster than an economy's capacity to produce. With more buyers than available goods, sellers can raise prices without losing sales, and the pressure shows up across many categories at once.
cards.example: The Federal Reserve's own history of the Great Inflation records that inflation measured a little more than 1 percent a year in 1964 and reached more than 14 percent in 1980 - a build-up over sixteen years, not a single bad quarter.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.observationPeriod: 1964 and 1980, within the 1965-1982 Great Inflation

cards.title: Cost-Push Inflation
cards.definition: Cost-push inflation happens when producing goods and services becomes more expensive - because energy, raw materials, or wages cost more - and firms pass some of that increase into their prices. Output tends to fall at the same time, which is what makes it hard for policy to offset.
cards.example: The Arab oil embargo that began in October 1973 lasted about five months and quadrupled crude oil prices. Energy is an input to almost everything, so a shock in one commodity raised the price of groceries, plastics, and airfares alike.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.geography: United States and global oil market

cards.title: Hyperinflation
cards.definition: Hyperinflation is inflation so rapid that money stops working as a store of value and, eventually, as a means of payment. Economists conventionally mark it off from ordinary high inflation at more than 50 percent per month - a threshold proposed by Phillip Cagan in 1956, not a legal definition.
cards.example: In Germany in 1923 wages were paid daily in many places, because by evening the morning's notes bought less. When the Rentenmark replaced the Mark that November, the entire German war debt of 154 billion Mark was worth 15.4 Pfennig.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Deflation
cards.definition: Deflation is a sustained fall in the general price level. It can be damaging rather than welcome: if households and firms expect prices to keep falling they postpone purchases, and the real burden of debts already taken on rises.
cards.example: Japan spent years with inflation near or below zero before the Bank of Japan set an explicit price stability target of 2 percent in January 2013. A shopper who waits for next month's lower price is behaving rationally and starving the economy of demand at the same time.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The 2 Percent Goal
cards.definition: Many central banks aim for a low but positive inflation rate rather than zero. A small buffer leaves room to cut interest rates in a downturn before they hit their lower bound, and it reduces the chance of tipping into deflation.
cards.example: Before January 2012 markets had to infer the Fed's target from how it behaved. Publishing the number changed that: the 2 percent goal itself became the anchor, and the Committee's 2025 framework review left it in place.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Interest Rates
topics.summary: What interest rates are, who sets the benchmark, and how a rate change travels through the economy.

cards.title: What an Interest Rate Is
cards.definition: An interest rate is the price of borrowing money, quoted as a percentage per year. Borrowers pay it and lenders receive it. It compensates the lender for giving up the use of the money and for the risk that it is not repaid in full.
cards.example: The same borrower faces many prices at once. On any given day the Fed's H.15 release shows an overnight bank loan, a 3-month Treasury bill, and a 30-year Treasury bond all carrying different rates - the longer the money is tied up, the more is usually charged for it.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

cards.title: The Federal Funds Rate
cards.definition: The federal funds rate is the rate at which banks lend reserve balances to one another overnight. The Federal Open Market Committee sets a target range for it, and that range anchors a wide set of other borrowing and saving rates.
cards.example: In March 2020 the Committee cut the range to 0 to 0.25 percent. By 27 July 2023 it had raised the upper limit to 5.50 percent and left it there for about a year - the steepest climb in four decades, and every card rate and savings rate in the country moved with it.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)
source.documentTitle: Federal Funds Target Range - Upper Limit (DFEDTARU)

claim.observationPeriod: March 2020 through 27 July 2023

cards.title: Real and Nominal Rates
cards.definition: The nominal rate is the rate quoted on a loan or a deposit. The real rate subtracts inflation from it. When the nominal rate sits below the inflation rate the real rate is negative: the balance grows in currency terms while buying less than it did.
cards.example: The Treasury sells 2 kinds of note side by side: an ordinary one, and an inflation-protected one whose principal rises with the CPI. The gap between what buyers accept on each is the market saying out loud how much inflation it expects.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: U.S. Department of the Treasury, TreasuryDirect

cards.title: How Higher Rates Slow Inflation
cards.definition: Raising the policy rate raises borrowing costs across the economy. Households and firms borrow and spend less, demand cools, and firms find price increases harder to make stick. The effect works with a lag usually measured in quarters rather than weeks.
cards.example: The chain is long and slow. A rate decision in March changes what a builder pays for a construction loan in June, how many houses get framed by September, and how many framing crews are hired after that. The Fed is steering something with a very long wheelbase, and the full effect of one decision can take 4 to 6 quarters to arrive.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

cards.title: The Yield Curve
cards.definition: The yield curve plots government bond yields against their maturities. Longer maturities normally yield more. When short-term yields exceed long-term ones the curve is inverted, a pattern that has often, though not always, preceded U.S. recessions.
cards.example: The 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread first went negative on 1 April 2022, turned negative again that July, and did not close above zero for good until 6 September 2024. Lenders were being paid less to tie money up for a decade than for two years.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Lower Bound
cards.definition: Policy rates cannot fall far below zero, because holding physical cash always pays zero. Once a central bank reaches this lower bound and still wants to ease, it turns to other tools such as asset purchases and explicit communication about future rates.
cards.example: The Federal Reserve sat at the bound twice in a dozen years: from December 2008 to December 2015, and again from March 2020 to March 2022. In both stretches it had to reach for other tools because the rate lever had stopped moving.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Consumer Borrowing Costs
cards.definition: Policy rate changes do not reach all consumer credit equally or at the same speed. Rates on revolving credit tend to reprice quickly, while a fixed-term loan already taken out does not change at all - only new borrowing does.
cards.example: One household, two loans, opposite outcomes: a car loan signed in 2021 keeps its 2021 rate for the whole term no matter what the Fed does afterwards, while the credit card in the same wallet can reprice within a billing cycle or two.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Negative Policy Rates
cards.definition: A few central banks have set a policy rate below zero, charging banks to hold excess reserves rather than paying them. The aim is to push banks toward lending. The approach is contested and its effects are still debated.
cards.example: The European Central Bank's deposit facility rate went below zero on 11 June 2014 and stayed there for 8 years, returning to 0.00 percent on 27 July 2022. For that stretch a bank parking spare cash at the ECB paid for the privilege.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: GDP
topics.summary: What gross domestic product counts, how it is built up, and what it deliberately leaves out.

cards.title: What GDP Measures
cards.definition: Gross domestic product is the market value of the final goods and services produced within a country during a period. It is a measure of production. It is not a measure of wealth, of wellbeing, or of how output is shared.
cards.example: Only the final sale counts. When a mill sells flour to a bakery and the bakery sells bread, GDP records the bread, not both - otherwise the flour would be counted twice. BEA publishes the result in 3 successive estimates per quarter as fuller data arrive.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Four Components
cards.definition: GDP is commonly written as consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports. Net exports are negative when a country imports more than it exports, which subtracts from the total without meaning the economy shrank.
cards.example: One component dwarfs the rest. Personal consumption expenditures have run near 68 percent of U.S. GDP in recent quarters, which is why a change in household spending moves the headline more than anything a government or an exporter does.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Real and Nominal GDP
cards.definition: Nominal GDP values output at the prices of the period, so it rises when prices rise. Real GDP holds prices fixed at a base year so that changes reflect actual production. Real GDP is the series used to judge growth.
cards.example: An economy producing exactly the same goods in 2 successive years, at prices 10 percent higher in the second, would post 10 percent nominal growth and zero real growth. FRED labels the real series in chained 2017 dollars precisely so the two cannot be confused.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: GDP Per Capita
cards.definition: GDP per capita divides output by population. It is a rough comparison of average economic output per person, and it says nothing about how that output is distributed within a country.
cards.example: Two countries with identical GDP per capita can look nothing alike: one where most people earn near the average, another where a few earn far above it and most far below. The World Bank publishes the underlying totals for over 200 economies; the averaging happens afterwards, and hides everything inside it.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Two Quarters Is a Rule of Thumb
cards.definition: The idea that two consecutive quarters of falling GDP constitute a recession is a shorthand, not the official U.S. standard. It is convenient because it uses one series, and unreliable for the same reason.
cards.example: The 2020 downturn makes the point. NBER dated a recession lasting 2 months, from a February 2020 peak to an April 2020 trough - far too short to produce two consecutive negative quarters, yet unmistakably a recession by every other measure.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.observationPeriod: February 2020 peak to April 2020 trough

cards.title: Annualized Growth
cards.definition: U.S. quarterly GDP growth is usually reported at an annual rate: the quarter's change compounded as though it continued for a full year. A quarterly change of about half a percent is reported as roughly 2 percent.
cards.example: This is why a U.S. and a European growth headline cannot be compared as printed. The same quarter of output growth is reported at roughly 4 times the size in Washington as in Frankfurt, purely because of the reporting convention.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.observationPeriod: BEA quarterly GDP reporting convention (as published on 2026-08-30)

cards.title: GDP and GNP
cards.definition: GDP counts production inside a country's borders whoever owns the factors of production. Gross national product counts production by a country's residents wherever it occurs. The two diverge most for economies with large cross-border income flows.
cards.example: A Japanese-owned car plant in Ohio adds to U.S. GDP because the cars are built on U.S. soil, and to Japan's GNP to the extent its profits flow to Japanese owners. BEA publishes the 2 measures plus the income flows that reconcile them.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: What GDP Leaves Out
cards.definition: GDP counts market transactions. Unpaid household and care work, volunteering, and the depletion of natural resources sit largely outside it, and spending to repair damage adds to GDP without leaving anyone better off.
cards.example: A parent who leaves a job to raise a child reduces measured GDP twice over: 1 salary disappears, and so does the paid childcare they no longer buy. The work went up, not down. This follows from the definition, which is why BEA's primer sets out exactly what is in scope.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Supply & Demand
topics.summary: How prices emerge from buyers and sellers, and what happens when shocks or policy push them around.

cards.title: The Law of Demand
cards.definition: Holding other things equal, a higher price leads buyers to purchase less of a good and a lower price leads them to purchase more. Drawn on a chart, that relationship is the downward-sloping demand curve.
cards.example: Households substitute rather than simply going without: when beef gets expensive, chicken shows up on more plates. BLS re-measures those choices through the Consumer Expenditure Surveys, which run 2 collections - an interview survey and a diary - to catch both big purchases and small ones.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Law of Supply
cards.definition: Holding other things equal, a higher price leads producers to offer more of a good, because more units become profitable to produce. Drawn on a chart, that relationship is the upward-sloping supply curve.
cards.example: Supply cannot always answer. A factory already running 3 shifts cannot add a fourth, and that ceiling is measurable: the Fed's G.17 release reports capacity utilization alongside output, showing how much room a higher price still has to work with.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
source.documentTitle: G.17 Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization

cards.title: Equilibrium
cards.definition: Equilibrium is the price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. Markets tend toward it, but shocks and slow-moving supply mean observed prices spend much of their time away from it.
cards.example: Housing shows how slowly the adjustment can run. A price signal in 2021 reaches a permit, then a start, then a completed house - 3 separate steps that Census reports as separate monthly series, and often years apart from end to end.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Price Elasticity
cards.definition: Elasticity measures how much quantity responds to a price change. Demand is elastic when a small price change causes a large change in quantity, and inelastic when it barely moves. Necessities without close substitutes tend to be inelastic.
cards.example: Shelter is the least avoidable thing most households buy, and the CPI weights it accordingly: a 1 percent move in shelter shifts the index far more than a 1 percent move in a category people can skip, because the weights come from what households actually spend.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Supply Shocks
cards.definition: A supply shock is a sudden change in the availability or cost of an input. An adverse shock raises prices and reduces output at the same time, which is why it is harder for policy to offset than a shift in demand.
cards.example: The 1979 energy crisis tripled the cost of oil. Prices rose and output fell together, which left policymakers with no comfortable move: cooling demand deepened the slump, and supporting demand fed the prices.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Price Ceilings
cards.definition: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. Set below the market-clearing level it holds prices down for whoever can buy at the cap while reducing the quantity supplied, which surfaces as shortages, queues, or a fall in quality.
cards.example: On 15 August 1971 the United States froze wages and prices across the whole economy for 90 days. Measured inflation duly fell while the freeze held, and resumed once the controls were relaxed - the price had been covered up, not brought down.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Price Floors
cards.definition: A price floor is a legal minimum price. The minimum wage is the most familiar example. Set above the market-clearing level, a floor raises pay for those who keep their jobs, while the size and direction of any employment effect remains actively debated among economists.
cards.example: A floor only bites where pay is already below it. In a labour market where employers are competing above the minimum, raising it changes nothing for most workers - which is why BLS publishes average hourly earnings every month alongside the 2 employment surveys.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Substitutes and Complements
cards.definition: Two goods are substitutes when a price rise for one increases demand for the other, and complements when they are used together, so that a price rise for one reduces demand for the other.
cards.example: Petrol and large cars are complements: when fuel costs jump, showrooms full of thirsty vehicles go quiet. Coffee and tea are substitutes. BLS catches both effects by re-weighting the CPI basket from the 2 expenditure surveys rather than assuming buying habits are frozen.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Labor Markets
topics.summary: How employment and unemployment are counted, and what the monthly jobs data can and cannot tell you.

cards.title: The Unemployment Rate
cards.definition: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people divided by the labor force. To be counted as unemployed a person must be without a job, available for work, and have actively looked for work in the prior four weeks.
cards.example: Someone who searches for 6 months, gives up, and stops looking leaves the labor force entirely - and the unemployment rate falls. Nothing improved. The definition counts searching, not wanting.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Labor Force Participation
cards.definition: The labor force participation rate is the share of the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over that is either working or actively looking for work. It captures people the unemployment rate does not.
cards.example: Between February and April 2020 participation fell from 63.3 percent to 60.1 percent. Millions had not become unemployed in the official sense - they had stopped looking, which is why the two rates must be read together.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)

claim.observationPeriod: February 2020 and April 2020

cards.title: Frictional Unemployment
cards.definition: Some unemployment is the ordinary churn of a working labor market: people leaving one job before starting another, and new entrants searching for a first job. This is frictional unemployment, and it does not fall to zero in a healthy economy.
cards.example: A graduate who spends 6 weeks choosing between offers is unemployed by the official definition and in no economic distress at all. BLS reports duration of unemployment each month so this churn can be told apart from long-term joblessness.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Structural Unemployment
cards.definition: Structural unemployment arises when the skills, locations, or industries of job seekers do not match the jobs on offer. Unlike frictional unemployment it can persist for years, and it is resolved by retraining or relocation rather than by faster searching.
cards.example: A mill town where the mill closed can have vacancies 200 miles away and still nobody working. Cheaper credit does not move a family or teach a trade, which is the limit the Fed's own explainer draws around what interest rates can fix.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
source.documentTitle: Monetary Policy: What Are Its Goals? How Does It Work?

cards.title: The Phillips Curve
cards.definition: The Phillips curve describes an observed short-run relationship between labor market slack and inflation: when unemployment is very low, wage and price pressure tends to build. The relationship has proved unstable over time and is not a dependable rule.
cards.example: The 1970s broke the rule outright - high unemployment and high inflation together, which the curve said should not happen. The Fed's history of the period treats that overconfidence as one cause of a 17-year inflation.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Contract and Self-Employed Work
cards.definition: Not all work is a traditional employer-employee job. Independent contractors, freelancers, and on-call workers are classified differently across statistical programs, which is why estimates of how many people work this way vary widely by definition and by source.
cards.example: A driver working 10 hours a week through an app and a full-time consultant may land in the same headline count or in neither, depending on whose definition is used. BLS measures the arrangements through the Current Population Survey; a platform's own user count is answering a different question.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Wages, Prices, and Productivity
cards.definition: Wage growth is not automatically inflationary. If pay rises roughly in line with productivity, the labor cost of each unit of output is stable and firms need not raise prices. Sustained wage growth well above productivity growth is what puts pressure on prices.
cards.example: A worker paid 4 percent more who also produces 4 percent more costs the employer nothing extra per unit sold, so nothing needs to reach the price tag. BLS publishes average hourly earnings monthly, which is where the pay side of that comparison comes from.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.observationPeriod: unit labor cost identity; BLS publishes average hourly earnings monthly

cards.title: The Monthly Jobs Report
cards.definition: The Employment Situation report combines two separate surveys: a survey of households, which produces the unemployment rate, and a survey of employers, which produces payroll job counts. The two can point in different directions in any single month.
cards.example: A person holding 2 jobs counts twice in the payroll survey and once in the household survey. That alone can send the two headlines opposite ways in the same month, and the payroll figure is then revised in each of the next 2 releases.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Trade & Tariffs
topics.summary: Why countries trade, what tariffs actually do, and how trade balances are measured.

cards.title: Comparative Advantage
cards.definition: Countries gain from trade by specializing where their opportunity cost is lowest, not where they are absolutely best. Even a country that produces everything more efficiently gains by concentrating on what it gives up least in order to make.
cards.example: The WTO sets it out with 2 countries: if A is better at cars and B is better at bread, both gain by specializing and trading. The harder case is a country worse at everything - and it still gains, by concentrating where its disadvantage is smallest.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.documentTitle: Understanding the WTO: The Case for Open Trade

cards.title: What a Tariff Is
cards.definition: A tariff is a tax on imported goods, paid to the importing country's government by the importer of record. It raises the landed cost of a foreign good. How much of that increase reaches the final price depends on who absorbs it along the chain.
cards.example: WTO members also publish ceiling rates they promise not to exceed, called bindings. As the WTO puts it, promising not to raise a barrier can matter as much as lowering one, because a firm signing a 5-year supply contract needs to know the rate will still be there in year 5.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.documentTitle: Understanding the WTO: Principles of the Trading System

cards.title: Trade Deficits
cards.definition: A trade deficit means a country imported more goods and services than it exported over a period. In the balance of payments it is matched by an offsetting flow on the financial account, so on its own it is an accounting fact rather than a verdict on economic health.
cards.example: The headline nets 2 flows moving opposite ways: the United States runs a large deficit in goods while running a surplus in services such as travel, finance, and software licensing. FRED's monthly balance has been negative in all 414 months it covers, back to January 1992.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Trade Agreements
cards.definition: A free trade agreement lowers or removes tariffs and other barriers among its members, and typically sets rules on origin, standards, and dispute settlement. Coverage is negotiated sector by sector, so no agreement removes every barrier.
cards.example: The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement entered into force on 1 July 2020, replacing NAFTA. Its rules of origin decide whether a car assembled in Mexico from parts made in 3 countries counts as North American at all - which is where most of the negotiation went.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The WTO
cards.definition: The World Trade Organization administers multilateral trade rules and provides a forum in which members negotiate and settle disputes. It does not set tariffs; members do, within the ceilings they have agreed.
cards.example: The WTO began life on 1 January 1995, but the system it inherited is older: the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade had been providing the rules since 1948. The organisation was new; the rulebook was not.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Protection and Its Costs
cards.definition: Protection shields a domestic industry from foreign competition using tariffs, quotas, or regulation. The benefits are concentrated in the protected industry, while the costs are spread thinly across buyers, downstream industries, and exporters who face retaliation.
cards.example: The WTO's own case for open trade puts it bluntly: protection "ultimately leads to bloated, inefficient producers supplying consumers with outdated, unattractive products." The 2 groups that notice are the protected firm, and - much later, after the subsidies have been paid - everyone else.

cards.title: Exchange Rates and Trade
cards.definition: A stronger domestic currency makes exports more expensive abroad and imports cheaper at home; a weaker one does the reverse. Currency movements therefore shift trade flows independently of tariffs or productivity.
cards.example: The broad dollar index rose from about 115 at the end of 2021 to about 128 on 26 September 2022. Nothing changed inside U.S. factories that year; their goods simply got more expensive for every foreign buyer.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Supply Chains and Resilience
cards.definition: Concentrating production wherever it is cheapest lowers cost and raises exposure to a single disruption. Diversifying or relocating production buys resilience by giving up some of that efficiency. It is a deliberate trade, not a free improvement.
cards.example: The New York Fed built the Global Supply Chain Pressure Index to put a number on the disruption. Its staff report finds recent inflationary pressures closely related to the index, especially in producer prices in the United States and the euro area - 2 economies, one shared bottleneck.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Housing Market
topics.summary: Why housing behaves unlike other markets, and how prices, rates, and construction interact.

cards.title: Why Housing Is Different
cards.definition: Housing is both a consumption good and a long-lived asset, it cannot be moved, it takes years to build, and it is usually bought with borrowed money. Those four features together make housing markets slow to adjust and prone to long swings.
cards.example: The Case-Shiller national index is set to 100 in January 2000, so its level reads straight off as a multiple of year-2000 prices. No other consumer purchase gets tracked this way, because no other one is simultaneously a place to sleep and the largest asset a household owns.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Rates and Affordability
cards.definition: A mortgage payment depends on the loan amount and the interest rate together. When rates rise, the payment on a given price rises with them, so the price a buyer can carry at a fixed monthly payment falls even if listed prices have not moved at all.
cards.example: The 30-year fixed average hit 2.65 percent in the week of 7 January 2021 - the lowest in a survey running since April 1971. Buyers who locked that rate and buyers shopping a few years later were looking at the same houses and completely different monthly payments.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Supply Responds Slowly
cards.definition: New housing arrives through permitting, starting, and completing construction, a pipeline measured in quarters and years. Demand can change in weeks. That mismatch is why price pressure appears long before any new unit does.
cards.example: A buyer who decides to move in March can be bidding by April. A builder who decides to add homes in March may pull a permit that summer, break ground the following year, and hand over keys the year after that. Census reports the 3 stages separately because they are that far apart.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The 2007-09 Housing Bust
cards.definition: A long rise in house prices financed by loosening credit standards reversed once prices stopped rising. Falling prices left borrowers owing more than their homes were worth, defaults climbed, and the losses spread through the financial system.
cards.example: Housing starts fell from an annual rate of about 2.27 million units in January 2006 to about 478,000 in April 2009 - the lowest reading in the whole series. Construction did not slow down; it very nearly stopped.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Rate Lock-In Effect
cards.definition: A homeowner holding a low fixed-rate mortgage gives it up by selling. When market rates are much higher, moving means a materially larger payment on a comparable home, so fewer owners list. Fewer listings tighten supply even while demand is falling.
cards.example: An owner holding a 3 percent mortgage who moves to a similar house at 7 percent takes on a far larger payment for the same roof. Staying is the individually rational response, which is why listings dry up - and a market where nobody lists is a market with no supply, whatever demand is doing.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.units: percent (illustrative mortgage rates from the weekly survey)
claim.observationPeriod: Primary Mortgage Market Survey range spanned between 2021 and 2023

cards.title: Renting and Owning
cards.definition: Renting and owning differ in cost structure, not merely in price. Owning carries maintenance, property taxes, insurance, transaction costs, and the opportunity cost of the down payment; renting carries none of those and builds no equity. Which costs less depends on local prices, rates, and how long a household stays.
cards.example: A household moving again within 2 years may never recover the transaction costs of buying; one staying 20 years usually does. The CPI has to price both situations, which is why it measures owner-occupied housing through owners' equivalent rent rather than through sale prices.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.documentTitle: Consumer Price Index Frequently Asked Questions

cards.title: Who Owns Rental Housing
cards.definition: Single-family rental homes are owned by a mix of individual landlords and larger firms. The share held by large institutional owners is small nationally while being far more concentrated in particular metropolitan areas, so a national figure and a local one answer different questions.
cards.example: The same firm can be invisible in the national statistics and a major landlord in 3 or 4 specific metros. Census tracks tenure - who owns and who rents - through the Housing Vacancies and Homeownership series, which is where any credible share has to start.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Housing Starts as an Indicator
cards.definition: Housing starts count new residential units on which construction began. Because building responds to expected demand and to credit conditions, starts tend to turn before overall activity, which is why they are watched as a leading indicator.
cards.example: The series is reported at an annual rate, so a single month reads in the millions even though far fewer homes were begun. It is also noisy enough that one month can move 10 percent on weather alone, which is why the figure is read as a 3-month average.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.observationPeriod: monthly series reported at a seasonally adjusted annual rate

topics.name: Central Banks
topics.summary: What central banks are for, the tools they use, and why independence is built into their design.

cards.title: What a Central Bank Does
cards.definition: A central bank manages the supply of money and short-term interest rates, acts as lender of last resort to the banking system, and in many countries supervises banks. Its statutory goals are set by law rather than chosen by the bank itself.
cards.example: Congress gave the Federal Reserve 2 goals - maximum employment and stable prices - and they can conflict. Cooling inflation usually means slowing hiring, so the dual mandate is a standing instruction to trade one off against the other in public.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
source.documentTitle: Monetary Policy: What Are Its Goals? How Does It Work?

cards.title: Monetary Policy
cards.definition: Monetary policy is the set of actions a central bank takes to influence money and credit conditions in pursuit of its mandate. It works indirectly - through interest rates and financial conditions - on the spending and hiring decisions of everyone else.
cards.example: No central banker sets the price of a mortgage or a car loan. The FOMC moves one overnight rate between banks, and everything else - the mortgage, the car loan, the corporate bond, the hiring plan - follows or does not, which is why 1 decision can take a year to show up.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

cards.title: Asset Purchases
cards.definition: When the policy rate is already near its lower bound, a central bank can buy longer-term securities to push down longer-term yields. The purchases expand its balance sheet; letting holdings mature without replacement shrinks it again.
cards.example: The Fed's total assets went from about $4.2 trillion in late February 2020 to a peak of about $9.0 trillion on 13 April 2022. The balance sheet more than doubled in two years, because the rate lever had already run out of room.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Independence
cards.definition: Operational independence means a central bank chooses how to pursue goals set by law without needing political sign-off on each decision. The design exists because short-term political incentives and long-run price stability frequently pull in opposite directions.
cards.example: The design is structural, not a promise. Governors serve long, staggered terms so no single administration can replace the board at once, and 12 regional Reserve Banks sit alongside the Washington board rather than under it.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Lender of Last Resort
cards.definition: A solvent bank can still fail if depositors withdraw faster than it can sell assets at a fair price. A central bank lending against good collateral during a panic stops that liquidity problem from turning into an insolvency.
cards.example: Deposit insurance stops the run before it starts. The FDIC states that deposits are automatically insured to at least $250,000 at each insured bank - so a saver under that limit has no reason to queue, and a queue that never forms needs no lender of last resort.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: One Policy, Many Economies
cards.definition: A currency union sets a single policy rate for members whose economies may sit at different points in the cycle. One rate cannot be right for all of them at once, and members have also given up the exchange rate as a way to adjust.
cards.example: The ECB sets 3 key rates for the whole euro area, and since a decision in March 2024 steers the stance through the deposit facility rate. A member in a boom and a member in a slump get the identical rate, and neither can devalue its way out.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Forward Guidance
cards.definition: Forward guidance is communication about the likely future path of policy. Because long-term rates reflect expected short-term rates, credible statements about the future can move borrowing costs immediately without any change in the policy rate itself.
cards.example: A 10-year yield is roughly what markets expect the overnight rate to average over 10 years. So a sentence about next year can move a mortgage rate the same afternoon without a single vote being taken - which is why the FOMC publishes a statement, minutes 3 weeks later, and quarterly projections.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Central Bank Money and Payments
cards.definition: Central bank money is what banks use to settle payments with one another. Several central banks have researched issuing a digital form of it to the public, and design questions about privacy, bank funding, and access remain unresolved.
cards.example: When money moves between 2 banks, the banks settle in reserve balances held at the central bank - the layer beneath the app, invisible to whoever tapped a card. A digital currency for the public would extend that layer past the banks, which is precisely why it is contested.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Recessions
topics.summary: How recessions are dated, what tends to precede them, and how policy responds.

cards.title: What a Recession Is
cards.definition: In the United States a recession is dated by the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee as a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy and lasting more than a few months. The committee weighs depth, diffusion, and duration together.
cards.example: The committee dates turning points long after they happen. The COVID-19 recession ran from a February 2020 peak to an April 2020 trough - 2 months - and was announced well after it had already ended.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.documentTitle: US Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions

claim.observationPeriod: February 2020 peak to April 2020 trough

cards.title: Leading Indicators
cards.definition: Leading indicators are series that tend to turn before overall activity: new orders, building permits, jobless claims, credit conditions, and the yield curve among them. They give warning, not certainty, and have signalled downturns that never arrived.
cards.example: No single one is trustworthy, so The Conference Board combines 10 of them into one monthly index and publishes coincident and lagging indexes beside it. A signal that shows up in 1 component is noise; one that shows up across most of them is worth attention.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.units: count (components of the US Leading Economic Index)

cards.title: The Business Cycle
cards.definition: Economies move through expansion, peak, contraction, and trough, then expand again. The pattern recurs in market economies, but the cycles are irregular in length and in cause. They are not periodic.
cards.example: NBER's chronology runs back to 1854 and shows just how uneven it is: the expansion from June 2009 to February 2020 lasted 128 months, the longest on record, while the contraction that followed lasted 2. Nothing about the cycle is on a schedule.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Fiscal Stimulus in a Downturn
cards.definition: When the economy contracts, governments often respond with spending increases or tax cuts intended to offset falling private demand. Each response has to be legislated, so its size and timing depend on what lawmakers pass and when.
cards.example: None of it is automatic. Every COVID-era relief package needed a separate vote, and the money then landed inside fiscal years 2020 and 2021 - which is where Treasury's outlay figures let the actual size be checked against what was announced.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Fiscal Data

cards.title: Automatic Stabilizers
cards.definition: Some parts of the budget respond to a downturn without any new legislation. Unemployment insurance payments rise as more people qualify and income tax receipts fall as incomes fall. Both cushion demand automatically, and both reverse as the economy recovers.
cards.example: When unemployment went from 3.5 percent in February 2020 to 14.8 percent in April, benefit payments started rising the same month under laws already on the books, while income tax receipts fell on their own. Congress did not have to act for either to happen.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)

claim.observationPeriod: February 2020 and April 2020

cards.title: Recessions and Jobs
cards.definition: Unemployment usually keeps rising after a recession's trough. Firms delay layoffs while hoping conditions improve, then delay hiring while waiting for demand to be confirmed. Employment is a lagging indicator of the cycle.
cards.example: The 2007-09 recession ended in June 2009 by NBER's dating, with unemployment at 9.5 percent - and it went on rising for four more months, peaking at 10.0 percent in October 2009. For anyone looking for work, the recovery began well after the recession was officially over.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Soft Landing and Hard Landing
cards.definition: A soft landing means bringing inflation down without a recession. A hard landing means tightening so far that activity contracts. Threading between them means acting on data that arrive late, with policy that bites later still.
cards.example: The hard version is on the record. After Volcker's announcement on 6 October 1979 the federal funds rate reached a record 20 percent in late 1980, inflation peaked at 11.6 percent that March, and the economy was pushed into a severe recession.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: K-Shaped Recoveries
cards.definition: Recessions do not hit everyone equally, and recoveries do not lift everyone together. When some industries and households rebound quickly while others stay depressed for years, the paths diverge on a chart like the two arms of a letter K.
cards.example: Leisure and hospitality employed about 16.9 million people in February 2020 and about 8.7 million that April - nearly half the industry gone in two months. Work that could move to a laptop carried on, and the two groups spent the next years on completely different paths.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Debt & Deficits
topics.summary: The difference between a deficit and a debt, who holds government borrowing, and what interest costs mean.

cards.title: Deficit and Debt
cards.definition: The deficit is the gap between what a government spends and what it collects in a single fiscal year. The debt is the accumulated total of past deficits net of any surpluses. A shrinking deficit still adds to the debt.
cards.example: A government cutting its deficit from $2 trillion to $1 trillion is still borrowing another trillion, and the debt still grows. Treasury reports the 2 things on separate pages for exactly this reason - one is a flow, the other a stock.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Fiscal Data

claim.observationPeriod: fiscal-year deficit and cumulative debt as reported by Treasury

cards.title: Debt Relative to the Economy
cards.definition: A debt figure means little without a denominator. Comparing debt to gross domestic product scales borrowing to the size of the economy that services it, which is what makes comparisons across countries and across decades meaningful at all.
cards.example: U.S. federal debt went from about 63 percent of GDP at the end of 2007 to about 123 percent in the first quarter of 2026. The dollar figure alone would have said far less, because the economy underneath it grew too.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Who Holds the Debt
cards.definition: Government debt is held partly by the public - domestic and foreign investors, banks, pension funds, and the central bank - and partly by government accounts themselves, such as trust funds. The two categories are reported separately for good reason.
cards.example: A Treasury bond held by the Social Security trust fund and one held by a pension fund abroad are both national debt, but only the second was borrowed from outside the federal government. Treasury reports the 2 categories separately so they are not confused.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Debt Limit
cards.definition: The U.S. debt limit is a statutory cap on total federal borrowing. It does not authorize new spending. It constrains the Treasury's ability to pay for spending Congress has already enacted.
cards.example: The limit has existed since 1917, and the sequencing is what confuses people: Congress votes the spending first and the borrowing authority second. Refusing to raise the limit does not cancel the spending already approved; it just leaves the bill unpaid.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

claim.observationPeriod: statutory limit dating from 1917

cards.title: Debt and Growth
cards.definition: Higher government debt can raise borrowing costs and leave less room to respond to a future crisis. There is no established threshold at which debt mechanically reduces growth - claims of a single critical ratio have not held up - and the effect depends on the currency of issue, the maturity profile, who holds the debt, and what the borrowing financed.
cards.example: Two countries at an identical 100 percent of GDP can be in completely different positions: one borrowing in its own currency at long maturities to build infrastructure, the other in foreign currency at short maturities to cover current spending. The ratio is the same and tells you almost nothing.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Borrowing in Your Own Currency
cards.definition: A government that borrows in a currency it issues cannot be forced into default by an inability to obtain that currency. That removes one failure mode and leaves the others in place, since creating money to cover obligations shows up as inflation and as a falling exchange rate.
cards.example: The constraint is real, it just arrives as prices rather than as a missed payment. The Fed's history of the Great Inflation describes an economy where inflation reached more than 14 percent in 1980 - nobody defaulted, and savings were destroyed anyway.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Long-Run Budget Pressures
cards.definition: Programs whose costs depend on demographics - retirement and health benefits - grow as a population ages, because fewer workers support more beneficiaries. Long-run budget projections are driven mainly by those programs and by interest costs.
cards.example: The arithmetic is demographic, not political: when the ratio of workers to retirees falls from 5 to 1 toward 3 to 1, a pay-as-you-go program costs more per worker without anyone changing the rules. Treasury's spending breakdown shows how large those categories already are.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Net Interest
cards.definition: Net interest is what a government pays to service debt it has already issued. It rises when the debt grows, when rates rise, and as older low-rate securities mature and are refinanced at prevailing rates. Unlike most spending it is not discretionary.
cards.example: A bond issued at 1 percent in 2021 does not stay cheap forever. When it matures it is replaced at whatever rate prevails, so interest costs can climb for years after rates stop rising - with no vote taken and no program expanded.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Exchange Rates
topics.summary: What sets the price of one currency in another, and how exchange rates move through an economy.

cards.title: What an Exchange Rate Is
cards.definition: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. Quoting conventions differ, so the same rate can be written two ways - dollars per euro or euros per dollar - and reading it in the wrong direction inverts its meaning entirely.
cards.example: On 27 September 2022 the euro was worth about $0.96 - below parity, so a euro bought less than a dollar. Quoted the other way round the same fact reads as about 1.04 euros per dollar, and a reader skimming the number could easily conclude the opposite.

cards.title: Floating and Fixed
cards.definition: Under a floating rate the market sets the price and it moves continuously. Under a fixed or pegged rate the authorities commit to a level and defend it by buying and selling currency or by adjusting policy. A peg imports the anchor currency's monetary conditions along with its stability.
cards.example: On 15 August 1971 the United States ended the convertibility of dollars into gold, and the fixed parities of the Bretton Woods system unwound with it. The major currencies have floated against one another ever since.

cards.title: Reference Rates
cards.definition: Because currency trades happen continuously across many venues, official bodies publish reference rates: a single daily or weekly fixing used for accounting, contracts, and statistics rather than for trading.
cards.example: A company closing its books needs 1 number, not a day of ticks. The ECB publishes euro reference rates each working day and the Fed publishes its H.10 rates weekly, and neither is a price anyone actually traded at.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Size of the Market
cards.definition: Foreign exchange is the largest financial market by turnover and it is decentralized - there is no single exchange. Turnover is therefore measured through a coordinated survey of dealers rather than read off one venue's records.
cards.example: Because no exchange sees the whole market, the BIS counts it every three years by surveying dealers in dozens of jurisdictions at once. The April 2025 survey put global FX trading at about $9.6 trillion per day.

cards.title: The Dollar's Role
cards.definition: A currency can be used far beyond its home economy - to invoice trade, to borrow in, and as a reserve asset held by other central banks. That role makes its exchange rate matter for countries that do not use it at all.
cards.example: In the April 2022 BIS survey the U.S. dollar was on one side of 88 percent of all trades, against 31 percent for the euro. Shares are measured out of 200 percent because every trade has two currencies - and a Brazilian importer paying a Korean supplier will often route through the dollar anyway.

cards.title: Purchasing Power Parity
cards.definition: Purchasing power parity compares currencies by what they actually buy rather than by the market exchange rate. PPP conversion factors are used for cross-country comparisons of income and output, because market rates can sit away from relative price levels for years at a time.
cards.example: A haircut costs very different amounts in 2 countries and cannot be shipped between them, so nothing forces the market rate to equalize its price. Converting incomes at market rates therefore understates living standards where local services are cheap, which is why the World Bank publishes PPP factors instead.

cards.title: Trade-Weighted Indexes
cards.definition: A currency can strengthen against one partner while weakening against another, so a single bilateral rate can mislead. A trade-weighted index aggregates bilateral rates using trade shares to give one measure of a currency's broad value.
cards.example: A dollar that falls against the euro while rising against the peso has not obviously done either thing. The Fed's broad index, set to 100 in January 2006, resolves it by weighting each partner by how much the United States actually trades with it.

cards.title: Pass-Through to Prices
cards.definition: A weaker currency raises the domestic price of imports, and some of that increase reaches consumer prices. The share that passes through is partial and varies by country, by product, and with how long the move persists. It is never one for one.
cards.example: A 10 percent currency fall does not raise shelf prices by 10 percent. Importers absorb part of it in their margins, retailing and transport costs are domestic anyway, and buyers switch to local substitutes - so the effect is smaller than the move and arrives months later.

topics.name: Consumer Spending
topics.summary: How household spending is measured, what funds it, and why it dominates the U.S. economy.

cards.title: Consumption Drives the Economy
cards.definition: Personal consumption expenditures - what households spend on goods and services - are the largest single component of U.S. gross domestic product. A change in household spending therefore moves the whole aggregate more than a change in any other component.
cards.example: Consumption has run near 68 percent of U.S. GDP in recent quarters. That is why a shift in what households do with their money outweighs almost anything a single industry, exporter, or government program can do to the headline.

cards.title: Income, Outlays, and Saving
cards.definition: Household saving is what remains of disposable personal income after outlays. The personal saving rate expresses that remainder as a percentage of disposable income. It is an aggregate residual, not a survey of what households intend to put aside.
cards.example: In April 2020 the saving rate hit 31.8 percent, by far the highest in a series that begins in 1959. Households had not become thrifty overnight - shops were shut and payments had arrived, so income stayed and outlays could not.

cards.title: Retail Sales
cards.definition: Retail sales measure receipts at retail and food service businesses. They cover goods and restaurant meals but not most services, so they are an early and partial read on consumption rather than a complete one.
cards.example: Retail sales fell from about $468 billion in March 2020 to about $401 billion in April, a drop of roughly 14 percent in a single month. Census publishes an advance estimate about two weeks after each month ends, which is why this was visible long before the GDP figures.

cards.title: Durables and Nondurables
cards.definition: Spending on durable goods - cars, appliances, furniture - is postponable and usually financed, which makes it far more cyclical than spending on nondurables and services. Downturns show up in durables first and most sharply.
cards.example: A worried household can put off replacing a 9-year-old car for another year. It cannot put off groceries or rent. BEA splits consumption into durables, nondurables, and services precisely because those 3 behave so differently in a downturn.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Consumer Credit
cards.definition: Households smooth spending using credit. Revolving credit, mainly credit cards, can be drawn and repaid repeatedly; nonrevolving credit such as auto and student loans is drawn once and amortized. The two behave very differently over a cycle.
cards.example: A card balance can double in a bad month and be cleared in a good one; a 6-year car loan does neither. The Fed's G.19 release reports the 2 categories separately because a rise in one means something quite different from a rise in the other.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

cards.title: Household Balance Sheets
cards.definition: Spending capacity depends on balance sheets as well as on income: total debt outstanding, its composition, and how much of it is falling behind. Rising balances mean something different when incomes are rising than when they are flat.
cards.example: Rising card balances can mean confidence or distress, and the balance alone cannot tell you which. The New York Fed publishes delinquency transitions alongside balances every quarter, because the share of borrowers newly falling 30 days behind is what separates the 2 stories.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: What Households Actually Buy
cards.definition: Aggregate consumption totals say nothing about composition. Expenditure surveys ask households directly what they spend on, which is how spending patterns by income, age, and household size are established rather than inferred.
cards.example: Nobody remembers a year of coffees, so BLS runs 2 surveys: an interview for rent, cars and insurance, and a diary for the small frequent purchases people forget. Those answers also set the weights inside the CPI.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Sentiment and Spending
cards.definition: Surveys of consumer confidence record how households say they feel about their finances and the economy. Sentiment and actual outlays can diverge for long stretches, so a confidence reading is a supplementary indicator rather than a forecast of spending.
cards.example: Households have told surveys they felt terrible while their card spending kept climbing. The Conference Board treats expectations as 1 component among 10 in its leading index rather than as a forecast in its own right.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Taxes
topics.summary: How tax systems are structured, what the U.S. federal government taxes, and what the terms mean.

cards.title: Marginal and Effective Rates
cards.definition: A marginal rate applies to the next dollar of income. An effective rate is total tax divided by total income. In a bracketed system the effective rate is never higher than the top marginal rate, because earlier dollars are taxed in the lower brackets they fall into.
cards.example: A raise that crosses a bracket threshold is taxed at the higher rate only on the dollars above it; the earlier dollars stay in the 2 or 3 lower brackets they fell into, untouched - so a raise can never leave a household with less after tax, though the belief that it can is remarkably durable.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.documentTitle: Federal Income Tax Rates and Brackets

cards.title: Progressive, Proportional, Regressive
cards.definition: A progressive tax takes a larger share of income as income rises, a proportional tax takes the same share at every level, and a regressive tax takes a smaller share as income rises. The labels describe the pattern of the burden. They are not judgments about fairness.
cards.example: A flat sales tax on food is regressive even though everyone pays the same rate: a household spending 30 percent of its income on groceries pays a far larger share of income than one spending 5 percent. The rate is identical; the burden is not.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Payroll Taxes
cards.definition: Payroll taxes fund specific social insurance programs and are levied on earnings rather than on total income. They are typically split between employee and employer, and the employee's share is withheld from each paycheck.
cards.example: On a U.S. paycheck the Social Security line is 6.2 percent and Medicare is 1.45 percent, totalling 7.65 percent - and the employer pays the same again on top, which never appears on the payslip at all.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Taxable Maximum
cards.definition: Some payroll taxes apply only up to an annual earnings cap. Above the cap no further tax is owed for that program, which makes the tax proportional below the cap and regressive when viewed across the whole income range.
cards.example: A high earner can cross the Social Security cap partway through the year and watch that deduction vanish from every remaining paycheck - while the 1.45 percent Medicare line, which has no cap, keeps going all the way to December.

cards.title: Where Federal Revenue Comes From
cards.definition: Federal revenue is not one stream. Individual income taxes and payroll taxes together supply most of it, with corporate income taxes, excise taxes, customs duties, and miscellaneous receipts making up the remainder.
cards.example: For many households the payroll tax takes more than the income tax does - 2 levies on the same paycheck, and the smaller-sounding one is often the larger. Treasury reports receipts by source for each fiscal year, so the mix can be read rather than assumed.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Fiscal Data

cards.title: Deductions and Credits
cards.definition: A deduction reduces the income that is taxed, so its value depends on the taxpayer's marginal rate. A credit reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar, so its value does not. A refundable credit can produce a payment when it exceeds the tax owed.
cards.example: A $1,000 deduction saves a 12 percent-bracket taxpayer $120 and a 37 percent-bracket taxpayer $370. A $1,000 credit saves both of them $1,000. The same headline number is worth three times as much to the higher earner in one form and identical in the other.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Who Actually Pays
cards.definition: Legal incidence is who remits a tax. Economic incidence is whose income falls because of it. The two often differ, because the party remitting can shift part of the burden into prices or wages depending on how responsive buyers and sellers are.
cards.example: Tariffs are the clearest case. The importer writes the cheque to customs, so legal incidence is obvious; whether the cost lands on the foreign producer, the importer's margin, or the shopper depends on who can most easily walk away. 1 payer, 3 possible bearers.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development

cards.title: Tax Expenditures
cards.definition: Exclusions, deductions, credits, and preferential rates reduce revenue in much the way direct spending uses it. Budget analysts call these tax expenditures and account for them separately precisely because they never appear as outlays.
cards.example: A housing subsidy paid as a cheque is spending; the identical subsidy delivered as a deduction is forgone revenue. The household ends up in the same place, but only 1 of the 2 shows up in the spending totals - which is why they are tracked separately.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

topics.name: Fiscal Policy
topics.summary: How government taxing and spending decisions affect the economy, and what constrains them.

cards.title: What Fiscal Policy Is
cards.definition: Fiscal policy is the use of government spending and taxation to influence economic activity. It is decided through legislation, which makes it slower to enact than monetary policy but able to target particular groups, sectors, or regions.
cards.example: A central bank can only change the price of money for everyone at once. Fiscal policy can send support to 1 industry or 1 region and leave the rest untouched - which is its real advantage over a rate cut, and the reason it takes months to pass.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Fiscal Data

cards.title: Discretionary and Mandatory Spending
cards.definition: Mandatory spending is set by ongoing law and continues without annual action; discretionary spending is appropriated each year. Most U.S. federal spending is mandatory, which limits how much the annual budget process actually controls.
cards.example: This is why a government shutdown does not stop Social Security cheques. They are mandatory spending, already authorized by standing law, while the annual appropriations fight covers a minority of the 2 categories of outlay.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Fiscal Data

cards.title: Expansionary and Contractionary
cards.definition: Expansionary fiscal policy raises spending or cuts taxes to increase demand; contractionary policy does the reverse. The labels describe the direction of the change relative to what would otherwise happen, not the level of the budget.
cards.example: A government running a $1 trillion deficit that shrinks to $500 billion is still borrowing - and still tightening, because the impulse is the change. Treasury reports the deficit by fiscal year, which is what makes the direction visible.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Multiplier
cards.definition: A fiscal multiplier is how much output changes per dollar of spending or tax change. Estimates vary widely with the state of the economy, the type of measure, and how monetary policy responds. There is no single agreed value.
cards.example: A dollar spent when factories are idle and a dollar spent when they are already running flat out do not produce the same result - the first can add output, the second mostly adds prices. Because economists genuinely disagree, the Philadelphia Fed publishes the range of independent forecasts each quarter rather than 1 consensus number.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Crowding Out
cards.definition: Government borrowing competes with private borrowing for available savings. When the economy is at capacity, that competition can raise interest rates and displace private investment. When resources sit idle, the effect is smaller or absent.
cards.example: Whether it is happening is an empirical question with 2 published answers: Treasury yields in the Fed's H.15 release, and how much industrial capacity is actually in use in the G.17 release. Borrowing into a fully employed economy looks nothing like borrowing into a slump.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

cards.title: Timing Lags
cards.definition: Fiscal policy faces three lags: recognizing that the economy has turned, legislating a response, and the response actually reaching the economy. Together they can run longer than the downturn being addressed.
cards.example: The 2020 recession lasted 2 months and was dated by NBER long after it ended. A response designed once the downturn was confirmed would have arrived into a recovery - which is how well-intentioned stimulus ends up being poorly timed.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: The Fiscal Year
cards.definition: Government budget figures are reported on a fiscal year, which need not match the calendar year. Comparing a fiscal-year figure with a calendar-year one without adjusting produces a misleading result.
cards.example: The U.S. federal fiscal year runs from 1 October to 30 September, so spending announced in November lands in the fiscal year named for the following calendar year. Treasury reports revenue, spending, and the deficit on that basis.

cards.title: Monetary and Fiscal Policy Together
cards.definition: The two arms of macroeconomic policy are set by different institutions, with different mandates and different speeds. Their effects combine: a fiscal expansion into a tightening monetary stance produces a different outcome than the same expansion on its own.
cards.example: The 2 arms can cancel out. Congress can pass a spending increase to support demand while the FOMC raises rates to cool it, and neither institution needs the other's permission - the independence that keeps monetary policy credible also guarantees the two can pull against each other.

topics.name: Economic Indicators
topics.summary: The main data releases, what each one actually measures, and how to read them without over-reading.

cards.title: Leading, Coincident, Lagging
cards.definition: Indicators are grouped by timing. Leading series tend to turn before overall activity, coincident series turn with it, and lagging series turn after. No single indicator is reliable on its own, which is why composites exist.
cards.example: Building permits lead, payroll employment moves with the cycle, and the unemployment rate lags. The Conference Board bundles 10 leading series into one index and publishes coincident and lagging indexes beside it, so the 3 timings can be read together.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Seasonal Adjustment
cards.definition: Many series carry a regular within-year pattern - retail sales in December, construction in winter. Seasonal adjustment removes that expected pattern so consecutive months can be compared. Adjusted and unadjusted versions of the same series are not interchangeable.
cards.example: Retail sales always rise in December and always fall in January; reporting that as a crash would be useless. But the headline 12-month CPI change uses unadjusted data, because comparing a month with the same month a year earlier already handles the season.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.
